newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy car market sees hope glimmer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy car market sees hope glimmer.

text.p: Italy's long-suffering car industry saw some glimmers of hope on Tuesday from new car November sales figures, but the signs are so faint analysts said it was too early to predict a turn-around after four depressed years.

Italy's Ministry of Transport issued November new car registration figures showing a fall of 11.44 percent to 134,000 units from 151,313, but the data was distorted by a strike of Italian car delivery truck drivers in October last year.

Last year's strike caused October registrations to soar nearly 23 percent, and it was predicted November figures would fall back against a very strong month in November 1995, when sales soared as car deliveries poured back into show rooms.

Analysts who chose to combine both months to smooth out the strike's effect said October/November 1996 sales rose 3.5 percent from October/November 1995, and came after a string of declines seen through spring and summer months in Italy.

"This data should not be regarded negatively, and after a disappointing August and September this picture is consistent with a market showing a slight improvement," said car industry analyst Bob Barber at HSBC James Capel in London.

Barber said November 1995 sales were boosted 16 percent above trend by the effect of the strike so a fall of 11 percent in November 1996 was a mildly encouraging result, but it was too early to signal an improvement in the national car market.
Italian car research group CSP also saw some glimmers of hope for the industry despite the November sales fall.
Grouping the October and November sales together, the forecaster said:
"So we are looking at a picture of substantial stagnation but with a very slight positive trend," referring also to its own survey of Italian car dealers on the future trend in Italian car sales.

The European car industry hit its nadir in sales in 1993. While Europe's top three car markets -- Germany, France and Britain -- have all recovered strongly, the continent's fourth largest market Italy has struggled to escape from 1993 levels.

Indeed, car registrations in Italy for the first eleven months of 1996 fell 0.33 percent to nearly 1.63 million and look unlikely to match 1995 12-month level of 1.74 million cars. Most predict a slightly lower number of around 1.72 million new cars.

Car industry bodies took a negative view on the figures with car producers association Anfia saying the November data was very disappointing with price cuts and dealer incentives eating into profit margins. Importing body Unrae saw little positive from the figures and held its 1996 prediction at 1.72 million.

Italy's dominant carmaker Fiat underperformed the November market seeing group sales off 17.1 percent as its share of the Italian market slipped to 45.6 percent from 48.8 percent. While sales of Fiat marque cars slipped around 14 percent its upmarket subsidiary Alfa Romeo saw sales slide 44.4 percent.
Fiat shares closed off 1.92 percent at 4,300 lire at the day's lows in a slightly lower Milan share market.

Some car makers like German Mercedes and BMW, together with Ford, Rover and Citreon saw sales up, but Volvo, Saab, Peugeot and Renault fell, while Volkswagen saw sales off 27.6 percent but still held on to its place as Italy's top car importer.

At the weekend, Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi rejected introducing a special car buying incentive scheme in Italy to stimulate purchases and boost sluggish demand similar to schemes introduced recently in France.
